hypothesis: The 7B player's main question-phase failure is getting locked into long runs of near-identical questions that all get No/Unknown (bare: i16 18 straight No on 'delay/misunderstanding' variants, i72 13 No on where the note lay, i20/i36 Unknown chains), and its final answers contradict referee replies. If the turn prompt flags a 4-reply run without a Yes and asks for a different, more basic aspect (including whether a premise is really true), and the final prompt is preceded by the referee's Yes/No facts, then the Yes rate rises and the model reaches premise-level facts (e.g. 'is X actually dead/alive') it never asked in bare, giving final answers closer to the hidden story.
behavior_changes: Turn prompt: when the last 4 referee replies contain no Yes, append a note saying that line is not working, not to ask another variation, and to ask about a different, more basic aspect such as whether something the puzzle states or assumes is really true. The model still writes every question; nothing is vetoed or rewritten.

Final prompt: before AR-Bench's final_prompt, show the questions answered YES (true) and NO (false), with the leading 'Q:' stripped, and instruct that the answer must agree with every YES, claim nothing answered NO, and give one concrete explanation rather than a list of possibilities.
Verdict parsing accepts the referee's occasional 'A: Yes' / 'A: No' form.
preserved_behaviors: Official AR-Bench system prompt, 'Turn t' prompts, full chat history with raw referee replies, and AR-Bench's final prompt verbatim.
Model output is sent to the referee unchanged (the 'Q: ' prefix that the referee accepted at 0% not-a-question in bare); the final answer is the model's reply unchanged.
All 25 questions are used; temperature and max_tokens are unchanged; one LLM call per turn plus one final call (26 calls).
verification: Ran check_b0r0_cand_sp_strict1_b10g3r2_b0r0g0.py twice (before and after the 'A:' parsing fix): 10/10 status=ok, parsed_final_answer=True, 25 questions each, repeat 0%, not_a_question 0%, 26 calls each, no crashes.
Mean referee replies vs bare on the same 10 puzzles: yes 22.4% -> 32.0%, unknown 30.4% -> 22.0%, no 47.2% -> 45.2%.

Traces show the nudge redirecting the model to premise questions bare never asked: i16 'Is John still alive when he writes the letter? Yes' then a run of 9 Yes; i20 'Was Emily alive three days after the supposed plane crash? Yes' / 'Did Emily send the postcard herself? Yes'; i36 'Is Emma still alive? Yes'; i52 'Was Tom actually in the country? No'; i72 left the 13-question run on the note's location and moved to who left it (several Yes).

Longest run of replies without a Yes (bare -> candidate): i16 18->4, i20 15->4, i36 25->11, i5 20->10, i72 13->8, i82 12->4, i90 3->3, i93 5->4; worse on i52 5->15 and i94 4->14, where after an early lucky Yes (bare) the candidate's alternative hypotheses kept drawing No while the nudge fired every turn.

Final answers now build on the recapped Yes facts (i16: letter pre-written by someone close and sent exactly one week after the funeral; i72: left under the door by an acquaintance), but consistency is not guaranteed: i20 still asserts 'had access to Emily's identity' (answered No) and i94 asserts mind-reading (answered No).
risks: Once triggered, the nudge repeats every turn until a Yes arrives; on i52 and i94 the longest no-Yes run got longer than in bare (5->15, 4->14), so on some puzzles it can push the model off a line that a single follow-up would have confirmed.
The suggestion to question premises can draw trivially true Yes answers (i36 'Is Emma still alive?') that raise the Yes rate without adding information.
The recap lists whole questions, so the 7B sometimes copies NO-questions into the answer as if true (i20, i94) and writes long, list-like answers, which could hurt character-level F1.
Evidence comes from one batch of 10 puzzles with seeded/cached sampling; there is no outcome (F1) signal, so the Yes-rate gain is a proxy.
